newsitem.title: DENMARK: FEATURE - Danes find Viking, Middle Age shipwrecks in fjord.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Danes find Viking, Middle Age shipwrecks in fjord.

text.p: Danish archaeologists dredging a fjord near Copenhagen have uncovered a thousand-year-old Viking warship and the remains of seven mediaeval trading vessels, the biggest such find here for 35 years.
Dating from the 11th to the 14th centuries, the vessels were unearthed last autumn and this spring from the muddy bottom of Roskilde Fjord near Denmark's Viking Ship Museum.
Workers were digging out an island site for a new visitors' leisure centre when they found the wrecks.

"The discovery of the ships is sensational. They are the most important ancient shipwreck find in Denmark since the five Roskilde Viking ships in the 1960s," curator Morten Goethche, one of the project leaders, told Reuters.
In 1962, five 11th-century Viking vessels -- two warships, two trading vessels and a fishing boat -- were raised from Roskilde Fjord, west of Copenhagen.
They were pieced together and put on permanent display at the Viking Ship Museum in the cathedral town of Roskilde.
FINDS RAISE QUESTIONS ABOUT ROSKILDE'S PAST

"The new ship finds seem to have sunk in an area where there was a landing stage in the early Middle Ages. Some of them may have gone down during stormy weather, others had apparently been hauled onshore," Goethche said.
He said that no cargo had been found in the trading vessels, only logs for firewood, but that the finds were forcing archaeologists to reassess the importance of Roskilde as a commercial port.
"It had previously been thought that shipping died out in Roskilde at the end of the Viking period due to navigation problems in the fjord," he said.

"One new theory is that today's shallow fjord could in fact have been much deeper then, allowing shipping to unload directly at a jetty at Roskilde without having to transfer cargo to flat-bottomed barges as earlier believed."

Scholars had thought that Roskilde, its cathedral the traditional burial place of Danish monarchs, was superseded by Copenhagen as Denmark's capital in the late 12th century in part due to its better harbour facilities for big ships.
WARSHIP IS MOST EXCITING FIND

Although two of the 12th-century trading ships are the best preserved of the shipwrecks, the most exciting of the finds is the 11th-century Viking vessel, a typical, elegantly shaped, masted longship, with long, low hull and upper planking, three metres (10 ft) broad and with a 20-metre-long (66-ft) keel.
The distance between the ribs of the warship, of which about 40 percent remains, indicates that the vessel was propelled by 36 oarsman and had space for a 50-man crew in all.
The best preserved and biggest of the trading vessels, also 20 metres long but six metres (20 feet) broad, dating back to the 12th century and 50 percent intact, could carry 40 tonnes of cargo.
The other wrecks are in various states of repair but at least a third of most of the ships remains for the archaeologists to study.
Tests on the keels and planking show that the vessels, built largely of oak, were of local origin with one smaller, pine ship probably built in Norway.
To date, five of the wrecks have been partially excavated and visitors to the museum can follow the dig in progress and watch reconstruction work in a workshop.
The rest of the large trading vessel and parts of some of the lesser traders are to be raised from the fjord bed this year.
